title: Drought Is Why These Apps Exist
story: Herd Planner started with the drought. From 2020 to 2023, dry years cut the corn, the hay and the grass across cattle country. With too little to feed, ranchers sold cows, and the country's beef herd got smaller every year. I wanted tools that help a family see a dry year coming and decide early: how many head the grass can carry, how much hay they'll be short, and which cattle to sell first.
caution: Not all of the herd's drop was drought: the cattle cycle and prices played a part too.

chart.title: U.S. beef cows on January 1 (millions)
chart.change: 4.1 million fewer from 2019 to 2026, down 13% (our arithmetic from the NASS numbers)
chart.source: USDA NASS Cattle reports, released each January (2020 to 2026). Each year is the count as revised the following January; 2026 is the first estimate.

steps.title: Drought Spreads
steps.text: By March 2022, **61%** of the lower 48 was in drought, covering about **80%** of the beef herd.
steps.source: U.S. Drought Monitor, via Drovers, Mar 14, 2022

steps.title: Crops and Hay Come Up Short
steps.text: Nebraska, 2022: corn **165 bu/acre**, down 29 from 2021. Alfalfa hay **down 34%**.
steps.source: USDA NASS, via UNL CropWatch, Jan 13, 2023

steps.title: Feed Stays Short
steps.text: May 2023: U.S. hay stocks **26% below** the 10-year average. Nebraska pasture **68%** poor or very poor.
steps.source: Derrell Peel, Oklahoma State University Extension, May 16, 2023

steps.title: Ranchers Sell Cows
steps.text: 2022: beef cow slaughter **up 12.3%**. Cows and heifers were over half of all cattle slaughtered, the most since **1986**.
steps.source: Derrell Peel, Oklahoma State University Extension, Nov 28, 2022

steps.title: The Herd Shrinks
steps.text: **31.7 million** beef cows in 2019. **27.6 million** in 2026.
steps.source: USDA NASS Cattle reports, Jan 2020 to Jan 2026
